blocks.text: An oxide of hydrogen, water has the chemical formula H2O. This seemingly simple molecule has many surprising properties, which give it the status of "the medium of life". About two thirds of our bodies are water and we cannot exist without it. It is the most abundant compound in all organisms; its concentration varies from 65 to 89 percent in different organisms, and in multicellular organisms from tissue to tissue: bone cells are about 20 percent water and brain cells 85 percent. Water plays important roles in making and maintaining the matter of life (protoplasm) and in establishing the suitable environment necessary for the working of life.
Solvent properties

The ability of water to dissolve a wide variety of substances is due to two properties: the polarity of water molecules and their ability to form hydrogen bonds. The water molecule has distinct ends, each with a partial charge: the hydrogen atoms are partially positive and the oxygen atom partially negative. Such molecules are called polar molecules. The partial negative charge at one end of a water molecule is attracted to the partial positive charge of another; this weak attraction is a hydrogen bond, and water forms a network of such bonds. Many of the properties of water are due to its hydrogen bonds.

blocks.title: Without hydrogen bonding
blocks.text: Without hydrogen bonding, water would boil at minus 80 degrees Celsius and freeze at minus 100 degrees Celsius, making life impossible.

Because water molecules are polar, they gather around any other molecule that has an electrical charge, whether a full charge (ions) or a partial charge (polar molecules). When sodium chloride (a salt) is placed in water it breaks into positive (Na+) and negative (Cl-) ions, and these ions are surrounded by the opposite polar ends of water molecules. Similarly, when glucose is placed in water, water molecules form hydrogen bonds with the polar hydroxyl groups of glucose, and so glucose dissolves. Charged or polar molecules are therefore soluble in water. In solution, ions and molecules can react with each other easily, so water provides the medium for chemical reactions, that is for the metabolism of cells.

blocks.title: Hydrophilic and hydrophobic
blocks.text: Charged or polar molecules such as salts, sugars and amino acids dissolve readily in water and are called hydrophilic ("water loving"). Uncharged or non-polar molecules such as lipids do not dissolve in water and are called hydrophobic ("water hating").
Hydrophobic exclusion

Non-polar or uncharged molecules are insoluble in water because water molecules do not make hydrogen bonds with them. When they are placed in water, the water molecules move them out, and the insoluble molecules make hydrophobic associations with one another. Lipid molecules, for example, are insoluble in water; when they are excluded from water they make strong associations among themselves, which is why lipids help to maintain the membranes of cells.

Water molecules surrounding a sodium ion with their negative oxygen ends facing it. A drop of oil pushed together inside water, with water molecules around it.
blocks.caption: Polarity, hydrogen bonding, water as a solvent and hydrophobic exclusion (original diagram after Figures 4.6 to 4.9).
blocks.long_description: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons, so the water molecule is polar with a partially negative oxygen end and partially positive hydrogen ends. Each molecule hydrogen-bonds with its neighbours, which gives water its cohesion, surface tension, high specific heat and high heat of vaporisation. Around an ion such as Na+ the oppositely charged ends of water molecules gather, and the polar hydroxyl groups of glucose are hydrogen-bonded in the same way, so salts and sugars dissolve. Non-polar molecules such as oil cannot hydrogen-bond with water, so water pushes them together; this hydrophobic exclusion lets lipids associate and build membranes.

blocks.text: Heat capacity

Specific heat capacity is the number of calories (amount of heat) required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance from 15 to 16 degrees Celsius, that is by 1 degree. Water has a high specific heat capacity, 4.184 joules, which means it has a great ability to absorb and release heat with minimum change in its own temperature. Most of the heat energy absorbed by water is used to break the hydrogen bonds between its molecules; as the bonds break, individual water molecules move more freely and the temperature rises. Because of its high specific heat, water heats up slowly, and when given a cooler environment it holds its temperature longer. Water thus works as a temperature stabiliser for the internal environment of organisms and for their external environment.

blocks.title: How high is it
blocks.text: The specific heat of water is twice that of most carbon compounds and nine times that of iron.
Heat of vaporisation

The heat of vaporisation is the amount of heat required to change a liquid to a gas. Water has a high heat of vaporisation, 574 kilocalories per kilogram: a considerable amount of heat (574 kilocalories) is required to change 1 kilogram of liquid water into vapour, so water absorbs much heat while changing from liquid to gas. This property keeps the Earth's temperature moderate and gives a cooling effect to plants and animals when they transpire and perspire (sweat): every gram of water that evaporates from a plant or animal surface removes 574 calories of heat from the body.

blocks.title: A small evaporation, a real cooling
blocks.text: The evaporation of 2 millilitres of water out of 1 litre lowers the temperature of the remaining 998 millilitres by 1 degree Celsius.
Cohesion

Hydrogen bonds among water molecules enable them to "stick together". This attraction between molecules of the same type is cohesion, and water molecules have high cohesion. Plants depend on the cohesion of water for the transport of water and nutrients from roots to leaves: the evaporation of water from a leaf exerts a pulling force on the water in the xylem vessels of the leaf, and because of cohesion the force is relayed through the xylem all the way down to the roots, so water rises against gravity. Hydrogen bonds also give water a high surface tension: water behaves as if coated with an invisible film, which is why the insect water strider walks on water without breaking the surface.
Ionisation of water

When the covalent bonds among the atoms of a water molecule break, water ionises to form hydrogen ions (H+) and hydroxyl ions (OH-). Under normal conditions this reaction is reversible and equilibrium is maintained. At room temperature (25 degrees Celsius), in a litre of water one molecule in every 550 million is ionised, so the concentration of each of H+ and OH- in pure water stays at 10 to the power minus 7 moles per litre. H+ and OH- ions take part in many chemical reactions in cells, for example the hydrolysis of macromolecules. The relative concentrations of H+ and OH- determine the acidity and alkalinity of a medium, its pH, which affects biochemical reactions: enzymes work best at a specific pH.

blocks.title: Acids and bases
blocks.text: Acids combine with OH- ions, leaving H+ ions in the medium and making it acidic. Bases combine with H+ ions, leaving OH- ions in the medium and making it basic.
Maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius

Water shows its maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius, and its density decreases as the temperature falls below that, because the hydrogen bonds keep water molecules relatively far apart. When the temperature falls to 0 degrees Celsius water freezes, but the ice is less dense than liquid water, because at this temperature hydrogen bonding holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid. In rivers, streams and lakes, ice forms on the surface as the temperature falls; being less dense, it floats, acts as an insulator and does not allow heat to escape from the water beneath. In this way aquatic organisms are protected.

blocks.prompt: A pond freezes over in winter. Use two properties of water to explain why the fish beneath survive.
blocks.explanation: Ice is less dense than liquid water because hydrogen bonds hold the molecules further apart at 0 degrees, so it floats on top and insulates the water below. Water's high specific heat means the water beneath cools only slowly, so it stays liquid at a steady temperature for the fish.

blocks.text: Quick recap

items: Water is 65 to 89 percent of organisms and the medium of life. Its molecule is polar and forms a network of hydrogen bonds.
Solvent: polar and charged substances (salts, sugars, amino acids) are hydrophilic and dissolve; non-polar lipids are hydrophobic and are excluded, which helps build membranes.

High specific heat (4.184 joules) stabilises temperature; high heat of vaporisation (574 kilocalories per kilogram) cools by evaporation and moderates the Earth; cohesion lifts water up xylem and gives surface tension.
Ionisation into H+ and OH- (10 to the power minus 7 moles per litre each) sets pH; enzymes need a specific pH. Maximum density at 4 degrees means ice floats and insulates aquatic life.
